title: Rigatoni all'Amatriciana
subtitle: Rigatoni with guanciale, tomatoes, and pecorino in the Roman style
excerpt: Rigatoni all'amatriciana is the definitive Roman pork-and-tomato pasta: guanciale (cured pork cheek) rendered until crisp and fatty, tomatoes cooked briefly in the pork fat, then finished with pecorino. The sauce takes 20 minutes and has a depth of flavour that belies how few ingredients it uses.
sourceNotes: Amatriciana originates in the town of Amatrice in Lazio and is one of Rome's four canonical pasta sauces alongside carbonara, cacio e pepe, and gricia. The traditional version uses guanciale, not pancetta or bacon, and is finished with Pecorino Romano. The original Amatrice version uses no tomato (it was added in the 19th century when tomatoes arrived in central Italy).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made ahead and refrigerated for 2 days. Reheat gently with a splash of pasta water and toss with freshly cooked pasta.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian cured pork cheek, softer and fattier than pancetta, with a more pronounced pork flavour. The correct cut for amatriciana and carbonara.

content.text: Rigatoni all'amatriciana is one of Rome's four canonical pasta dishes. The sauce is

(cured pork cheek) rendered in its own fat, then tomatoes cooked in that fat. Pecorino Romano finishes it. Pancetta is sometimes used as a substitute but guanciale gives a noticeably softer, more unctuous result. The rule in Lazio is no onion, no garlic, no chilli in the base: these are optional additions, not the original.

Place the guanciale in a cold wide pan over medium heat. Let it render slowly in its own fat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has melted out and the lardons are golden and slightly crisp. If using chilli flakes, add them now. If using white wine, add it and let it evaporate, about 1 minute.

Add the tomatoes to the pan, crushing them with your hand or a spoon. Cook over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes until the sauce has thickened and the oil from the guanciale sits on top. The guanciale lardons should be distributed throughout. Taste and season: it may need very little salt.

Cook the rigatoni in well-salted boiling water until 1 minute short of al dente. Reserve a cup of pasta water, then drain. Toss the rigatoni into the sauce over high heat with a splash of pasta water for 1 to 2 minutes. Remove from the heat and stir in most of the pecorino. Serve topped with the remaining pecorino.

items.symptom: Guanciale is chewy rather than yielding
items.cause: Rendered too quickly over high heat, tightening rather than softening
items.fix: Start the guanciale in a cold pan and cook slowly over medium heat. The fat needs to melt out gradually.

items.cause: Using pancetta or bacon instead of guanciale, or the tomatoes were not reduced enough
items.fix: Guanciale has a distinct flavour from its cheek cut: use it when you can. Reduce the tomato sauce fully regardless of which pork cut you use.

items.cause: The pan was too hot when the pecorino went in
items.fix: Take the pan off the heat before adding the cheese. Stir vigorously: the residual heat from the pasta and sauce is enough to melt it.

content.text: Amatriciana comes from the Apennine town of Amatrice, north-east of Rome in Lazio, and the Romans claimed it as their own as waves of Amatricean workers settled in the city. It is now one of the city's four canonical pasta sauces. Amatrice was almost entirely destroyed in the 2016 earthquake, and the dish has since carried additional significance in Italy as a way of keeping the town's name and culture visible. The original bianca version (gricia) predates the tomato by several centuries.
